title: Lexington named
summary: In early June 1775, William McConnell's party camped at a spring on Elkhorn Creek. They named it Lexington after the April battle in Massachusetts.
bodyMarkdown:
Lexington got its name in early June 1775, when frontiersmen camping at a spring on Elkhorn Creek named it for the first battle of the American Revolution. That battle had been fought at Lexington, Massachusetts, on April 19.

The party, led by William McConnell, was surveying land along the forks of Elkhorn Creek in what is now Fayette County. Their camp was near a "sinking spring" on a branch of the creek, a spot known today as McConnell Springs. They hoped a town would one day grow there.

The Shawnee and their allies resisted Anglo-American claims to lands they used as hunting grounds, and once the Revolution began, many allied with the British. Their raids made the area dangerous, and permanent settlement waited four years. In 1779, Col. Robert Patterson and about 25 companions came from Fort Harrod and built a blockhouse near today's Main and Mill streets.

Cabins and a stockade followed. The Virginia General Assembly established the town of Lexington on May 6, 1782. McConnell Springs is now a city park, marked by state historical marker 554.

Sources: [Kentucky Historical Society, Marker 554: Lexington Named](https://history.ky.gov/markers/lexington-named); [Friends of McConnell Springs, Lexington & McConnell Springs History](https://mcconnellsprings.org/history-lexington-mcconnell-frontier/); [ExploreKYHistory, Marker 1637: Original Fort Harrod Site](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/977); [McConnell Springs in Historical Perspective](https://mcconnellsprings.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/McConnellSprings_in_Historical_Perspective.pdf)
